Daytime over the great island city of Tenochtitlan in the Valley of Anahuac, 1520. Camera stands on a high empty rooftop terrace near the centre of the city, roughly five storeys above the surrounding rooftops, looking out over the city as it falls away toward the lake. The city is entirely deserted in frame. From every direction below and beyond, thousands of women are wailing in grief, and the sound fills the whole valley.

FOREGROUND, lower quarter of frame: the near edge of a lime-plastered flat roof terrace, a low parapet of cut stone running across the bottom of frame, its plaster cracked and sun-bleached, held slightly soft. MIDGROUND, 40 to 200 metres: a dense field of flat-roofed single and two-storey lime-plastered houses in white, cream and pale ochre, packed tight, separated by narrow straight streets and by straight water canals with low stone embankments. Small stepped platforms and low shrines break the roofline. BACKGROUND, 300 metres to 2 kilometres: the broad open sacred precinct with the Templo Mayor rising out of it — a broad low stepped pyramid, much wider at the base than it is tall, with a single wide staircase up the front face and twin shrines standing side by side on the flat summit platform. Beyond the city, straight raised causeways run out across flat pale lake water to low dark hills on the far shore. Flat pale grey overcast sky over everything.

One continuous shot. Nothing in the city moves except the environment itself: a thin haze sitting in the middle distance at 20% density, faint smoke rising dead vertical from two or three cooking hearths somewhere in the rooftop field, the flat lake water beyond the causeways almost motionless. The camera makes its slow push and the city holds still under it.

AUDIO
Fully diegetic, no music of any kind. The dominant sound is a citywide wail of women's voices in grief — thousands of them, spread across every direction and every distance, layered on top of each other into one continuous unbroken mass of sound that fills the whole valley. No words, no chanting, no unison, no rhythm — each voice on its own timing, rising and falling independently, so the mass never resolves and never settles. The far voices smear together with distance into a single low continuous droning cry that sits under everything. Nearer voices cut through it individually and clearly at intervals: a raw open-throated scream, a long broken sobbing cry that runs out of breath and starts again, a high keening note held far too long. These near cries arrive from different directions and different distances, never in a pattern, sometimes two or three overlapping at once. The overall effect is enormous, inhuman in scale, and deeply unsettling — the sound of a whole city grieving at the same time, with nobody visible making it. Underneath, sparse city ambience: dogs barking somewhere far off, a single distant conch note, birds, water moving slowly in a canal. The wailing runs unbroken from the first frame to the last and never drops in intensity.

THE WEAPON — A HAND SLING, NOT A THROWN OBJECT
This is a SLING. It is the weapon David used against Goliath. It is a length of cord, and the stone is launched by whirling it on the end of that cord and letting go — the same principle as a hammer throw. It is NOT a thrown rock, NOT a bolas, NOT a net, NOT a whip and NOT a bag on a stick.

WHAT THE WEAPON LOOKS LIKE: a single length of braided plant-fibre cord about three feet long, with a small woven leather-and-fibre cradle at its midpoint that holds one stone. The cord has two halves — the half above the cradle and the half below it. The warrior holds BOTH cord ends together in ONE closed hand. The cradle with its stone hangs from that hand at the far end of the cord, about eighteen inches away.

HANDS: loading is two-handed — the off hand seats the stone into the cradle and then releases it. The whirl and the release are ONE-HANDED — the throwing hand holds both cord ends and does all of it alone, while the off hand hangs free and empty at his side. The off hand never touches the sling or the stone during the whirl or the release.

THE MOTION, IN ORDER — THIS IS THE CRITICAL PART:
1. LOADED AND HANGING. The stone sits in the cradle. The warrior holds both cord ends together in one closed hand. The loaded cradle dangles below or behind that hand at the full length of the cord. 2. THE WHIRL. He whirls his arm. The cord goes taut and the loaded cradle swings around his hand in a fast circle — over his head, or in a flatter arc beside his head. ONE or TWO fast rotations only. The cord is straight and taut with the stone's weight pulling outward.

THE WEAPON — A HAND SLING, NOT A THROWN OBJECT
This is a SLING. It is the weapon David used against Goliath. It is a length of cord, and the stone is launched by whirling it on the end of that cord and letting go — the same principle as a hammer throw. It is NOT a thrown rock, NOT a bolas, NOT a net, NOT a whip and NOT a bag on a stick.

WHAT THE WEAPON LOOKS LIKE: a single length of braided plant-fibre cord about three feet long, with a small woven leather-and-fibre cradle at its midpoint that holds one stone. The cord has two halves — the half above the cradle and the half below it. The slinger holds BOTH cord ends together in ONE closed hand. The cradle with its stone hangs from that hand at the far end of the cord, about eighteen inches away.

HANDS: loading is two-handed — the off hand seats the stone into the cradle and then releases it. The whirl and the release are ONE-HANDED — the throwing hand holds both cord ends and does all of it alone, while the off hand hangs free and empty at his side. The off hand never touches the sling or the stone during the whirl or the release.

THE MOTION, IN ORDER — THIS IS THE CRITICAL PART:
1. LOADED AND HANGING. The stone sits in the cradle. He holds both cord ends together in one closed hand. The loaded cradle dangles below or behind that hand at the full length of the cord. THE STONE IS NOT IN HIS HAND. His hand holds only cord. The stone is eighteen inches away from his hand, at the far end.
2. THE WHIRL. He whirls his arm. The cord goes taut and the loaded cradle swings around his hand in a fast circle — over his head, or in a flatter arc beside his head. ONE or TWO fast rotations only. Throughout the whirl the stone stays in the cradle at the end of the cord, circling around his hand. His hand stays roughly in place, gripping both cord ends. The cord is straight and taut with the stone's weight pulling outward.
3. THE RELEASE. At the top of the arc he OPENS his fingers and lets go of ONE of the two cord ends. Only one. That single end slips free of his hand. The cradle SNAPS OPEN and the stone launches out of it, forward and up, at high speed.
4. AFTER. The stone is gone. He is still holding the OTHER cord end in his hand, and the now-empty sling — cord and open cradle — whips out flat with his follow-through and then hangs slack and dangling from his hand. He is left holding a limp empty cord.

THE WHOLE SEQUENCE IN ORDER: stone resting in the cradle → he whirls the loaded sling around his hand → the sling accelerates → he releases ONE cord end → the cradle snaps open → the stone launches forward and away → the empty sling stays in his hand, still gripped by the other cord end.

The gunner stands at frame right of the cannon, close to camera and large in frame at one third of frame height, in rear view with his back to camera, one hand resting on the parapet stone, looking out over the plaza. His helmet and shoulders are the largest human forms in the composition.
The second soldier stands at frame left of the cannon, slightly further along the platform, also in rear view, both hands on top of the parapet, leaning slightly out over it and looking at the crowd.
Midground and background: the plaza beyond the parapet, its flagstones entirely hidden beneath the crowd, and the low platform temples and painted enclosures ringing it. The Templo Mayor stands at centre background, roughly 300 meters out — pure architecture, its steps and summit completely empty, nothing happening on it or at its base. Beyond, the precinct wall and a hazed line of distant mountains under heavy overcast.
Directly below the wall, the front of the crowd is already pressed against the base of the palace in a ragged uneven mass, faces turned up toward camera, arms raised, shouting upward.
Everything in frame is in motion from the first frame except the cannon carriage.

One continuous shot. The camera does not cut. There are no internal cuts, transitions, or angle changes at any point across the full 8 seconds.

OPTICS
Extreme wide shot, 84° FOV, rectilinear. Aperture f/11, deep focus — both soldiers and the falconet in the near foreground, the crowd across the entire plaza, and the Templo Mayor all hold readable detail simultaneously. Depth separation comes from atmospheric haze building with distance, not from defocus. No lens drift at any point.

Locked on a stable head, mounted, mechanically smooth — no handheld motion, no jitter, no tremor of any kind. A single slow dolly push forward at 0.6 km/h across the full 8 seconds, moving past the two soldiers so that the parapet and the cannon settle lower in frame as the plaza opens up. Both men stay large in frame and stay seen from behind throughout the move. The move is continuous and even from first frame to last, with no acceleration, no stop and no reframing. Height stays constant at 12 meters above the plaza floor. The Templo Mayor holds its position at the centre of frame throughout.
Tonal character: wide latitude, soft highlight roll-off across the flat overcast sky, deep retained detail in stone texture, dust, textile weave and the massed crowd.

ACTION
Across the full 8 seconds the packed mass drifts forward toward the palace wall at 2 km/h and never accelerates. Thin dust lifts off the flagstones under tens of thousands of shuffling feet and hangs low over the crowd.
Individual men throughout the crowd raise their arms, point up at the wall with open hands and shout upward — each on his own timing, isolated movements scattered randomly across the mass at random moments. Scattered warriors raise and shake their spears overhead, again each on his own timing and never together. Small local jostles and eddies form and dissolve continuously across the plaza.
On the gun platform the two soldiers begin bringing the falconet into service, working steadily and without hurry, both of them keeping their eyes on the plaza between tasks.
For the first two seconds both men are simply standing at the parapet looking out, holding still a beat longer than a man normally would.
The gunner then steps to the breech of the cannon, lifts a long swab out of the bucket of rammers with both hands, runs it down the bore in two slow strokes and draws it back out. He sets it against the carriage, then steps back behind the breech and sights along the length of the barrel out across the plaza, one hand resting on the elevation quoin under the breech, his back to camera the whole time. Once, near the end of the shot, his head drops to the crate of iron shot beside him and comes straight back up to the plaza.
The second soldier crouches to the shot crate, lifts a single iron ball out of it with both hands with visible effort, and sets it down on the timber beside the carriage where it settles heavily and stays put. He straightens, takes up the wooden linstock with the lit slow match coiled on it, brings the burning end close to his mouth and blows on it twice — the coal brightens to orange and a thin thread of pale smoke lifts off it and drifts across the near foreground. He plants the butt of the linstock on the platform, turns his head back to the plaza and stays there watching, his free hand going to the parapet stone.
Neither man leaves the gun platform, neither man steps back from the wall, and neither man turns his face to camera at any point. Neither soldier speaks.
By the end of the shot the crowd has advanced a few meters and packed harder against the base of the wall, the ball is sitting ready beside the carriage, and the slow match is burning with smoke lifting off it.

PERFORMANCE
The two soldiers play professional competence laid over dawning arithmetic — men doing small correct tasks with their hands while their attention keeps going back to the thing in front of them. It reads entirely through the back, the shoulders, the set of the neck and the timing of the head turns. No gesturing, no theatrical reaction, no flinching, no panic. The gunner's hands are steady on the swab and the quoin; his head comes back up to the plaza after every task, a fraction faster each time. The second soldier lingers at the parapet a beat too long before crouching to the crate, and stands square and still after he blows the match, both feet planted, weight forward on the stone.
The crowd plays collective anger held at a slow boil rather than battle frenzy. This is a city that has had enough, standing at the door of the people it has had enough of. Faces are furious, set, grim. Individual men shout upward, gesture and point at scattered moments, each on his own timing. Many people are simply standing packed in the mass, drifting forward, saying nothing at all. Nobody is chanting, nobody is marching in step, nobody moves in unison.
Skin, textile and dust render photographically: real woven fabric with visible weave and drape, brown skin under flat light, real dust, real pitted steel with worn edges on the two helmets, mail rings catching the flat light in dull broken points.

Tens of thousands of shuffling feet raise a thin low haze of dust off dry flagstone. Nobody has open ground to accelerate into. Capes hang and drape with small movements. Spear shafts stay rigid and sway gently at varied angles with the movement of the men holding them.
The iron ball carries real weight — it sits low in both hands, the soldier's arms and shoulders take the load, and it lands solid on the timber with no bounce and stays where it is set. The swab has length and mass and flexes slightly as it runs down the bore. The mail shirt hangs with real weight off the gunner's shoulders and shifts as he works. The slow match burns as a small live coal, brightening under breath and shedding a fine ribbon of smoke that drifts and thins in still air. The bulk of them — commoner levies and young warriors. A maxtlatl loincloth of plain white cotton wrapped between the legs and knotted at the front with two decorated ends hanging down. Bare chested above it. Many with a plain white or ochre tilmatli cape knotted over one shoulder, one or two in bright red. Some barefoot, some in sandals of woven hide straps. They carry the plain wood-and-cane round shield, the bow, the sling, and simple fire-hardened clubs.

The proven fighters — ichcahuipilli, sleeveless quilted cotton torso armor two fingers thick, layered unspun cotton stitched between cloth and bound at the edge with leather. Several cuts across the crowd: some tie at the back, some lace at the front, some pull over the head and hug the body to the top of the thigh, some flare loose to mid-thigh. Painted off-white, ochre, deep red and black, worn, salt-stained and torn open in places, a few trimmed with rows of short colored feathers at the hem.

The veteran ranks — tlahuiztli, close-fitting full-body feathered war suits covering torso, arms and legs, laced closed up the back, the feathers laid in tight overlapping courses over a quilted base. Solid fields of black, deep red, yellow, or blue-green quetzal. A few of these men carry a tall light cane back-frame rising off the shoulders, dressed with long green quetzal plumes or a stepped fan of feathers, swaying hard as they move. A few wear carved wooden helmets shaped as a stylised animal head, covering the skull and jaw with the face looking out of the open mouth.

The two elite orders, only a handful of men in the whole crowd — cuāuhtli eagle warriors in tawny brown and white eagle-feather suits with a wooden helmet carved as an open eagle beak, the man's face inside it; and ocēlōtl jaguar warriors in tight spotted jaguar-pelt suits with the pelt head worn as a helmet, teeth around the brow. Their shields are faced with dense feather mosaic.

A very small number of cuāuhchicqueh shorn ones — head shaved bare except for a single long braid or upright tuft over the left ear bound with red cord, body and face painted, pushing out ahead of everyone else.

THE WEAPON — TEMATLATL SLING, DESCRIBED PRECISELY
Each throwing warrior uses a hand sling made of braided maguey-fibre cord — a single cord roughly two and a half to three feet long with a small woven cradle or pouch at its midpoint. One end of the cord finishes in a loop worn over the middle finger of the throwing hand; the other end is a loose tail pinched between thumb and forefinger of that same hand. A rounded grey-brown stone the size of a tennis ball sits in the woven cradle. Each warrior has a cloth pouch of stones slung at his hip.

THE THROWING MOTION, IN ORDER: the warrior seats the stone in the cradle and lets the loaded sling hang. He swings his arm in ONE or TWO fast rotations — either up over his head or in a flatter sidearm arc — the loaded cradle blurring around the axis of his hand, the cord taut with the stone's weight. At the top of the arc he RELEASES the pinched tail end. The stone leaves the cradle instantly and flies away fast and flat, UP and PAST the camera and out of the top of frame in a blur. The now-empty sling whips out straight and flat with the follow-through and the loose cord trails and dangles from his hand as his arm carries all the way through.
This is a real weapon used with real technique, not someone waving a rope. The cord is taut and heavy while loaded and slack and light after release. The whole action is fast, athletic and violent. This is NOT a windmill of endless slow rotations — one or two fast turns, then release.

This must look like documentary footage of real people, not animation or a rendered game. Real human faces with asymmetry, blemishes, uneven skin, individual pores, stray hairs, imperfect teeth. THE STONES — HOW THEY MUST LOOK AND BEHAVE
The thrown objects are ordinary rocks — irregular chunks of grey and buff stone, rubble and broken paving fragments, roughly fist-sized, some smaller, none uniform. They are chipped, angular, dull and unpolished, every one a different shape. They are not smooth, not round, not spherical, not identical, not glowing, not oversized, not boulders.
They behave like real thrown objects under real gravity. Each one is thrown by a visible individual arm from a roof or a wall or across the water, follows its own separate ballistic arc, tumbles and rotates end over end as it falls, and accelerates downward. They arrive at different moments from different directions at different speeds — never in a synchronised volley, never in a uniform wave, never in formation, never all at once. Some fall short and clatter on the paving. Some go wide into the canal. A few strike home.
Impacts are hard and unglamorous: a flat metallic crack off a helmet, a dull thud off a padded shoulder, a sharp skitter and bounce across stone, a compact splash and expanding rings in the water. Stones bounce and roll after landing rather than vanishing. Dust puffs where they strike paving.
No slow-motion on any stone. No trails, no streaks, no glow, no impact flare, no debris explosion. They are just rocks falling out of the sky the way rocks fall.

HOW THE SPANIARDS MOVE — CRITICAL
Real marching, not animation. Every man's gait is his own — different stride lengths, different arm swings, different head carriage. They are not in step with one another. Boots land flat and heavy on stone and the body drops slightly into each step. Shoulders roll. Kit swings on the body a half-beat behind the man. Mail moves as a heavy hanging sheet, not as a solid surface. Men bump shoulders in the crowded ranks and correct. A man adjusts his belt as he walks. Another shifts a spear from one hand to the other. Someone stumbles slightly on uneven paving and recovers. The horse walks with genuine equine gait — four-beat, head nodding forward and back with each stride, hindquarters working, weight visible, hooves ringing on stone.
The column moves at a hard fast walk, roughly 7 km/h, quick and driven. Every Spaniard is frightened — eyes flicking up to the roofs and across the canal and back, jaws tight, hands near hilts.

THE NAHUA — PHYSICAL APPEARANCE, CRITICAL
Every person in this crowd is a full-blooded Indigenous Nahua of central Mexico in 1520, before any European contact. Their faces are the faces of living Indigenous Nahua people from the highland communities of Puebla, Hidalgo, Tlaxcala and Guerrero — unmixed Indigenous Mexican ancestry, the same lineage as the people who built this city.
SKIN: warm brown throughout, every single person — copper, russet, bronze, deep earth-brown. Nobody in this crowd is white, pale, fair-skinned, olive, Mediterranean, European, African, Black, Middle Eastern or Asian. Nobody is light-skinned. Nobody is mixed-race or mestizo. Every face is Indigenous American brown.
FACIAL STRUCTURE: broad face with wide prominent cheekbones set high and far apart. Broad flat forehead. Strong high-bridged nose with a wide base and full nostrils, some straight and some gently convex. Wide-set dark almond eyes with a pronounced epicanthic fold at the inner corner, irises dark brown to near-black. Full wide mouth. Heavy square jaw and a broad chin. Shovel-shaped upper incisors visible when the mouth is open.
HAIR: jet-black with a blue-black sheen, dead straight, thick and coarse, never wavy and never curled. Men wear a blunt fringe cut straight across the forehead with the rest long past the shoulders or gathered and tied at the nape. Women wear it long down the back, some braided and wound about the head with cords. Nobody has brown, blond, red or light hair. Nobody has curly, wavy or loose-textured hair.
FACIAL HAIR: none whatsoever on any man. Completely smooth bare skin at the upper lip, cheeks, jaw, chin and throat — genuinely hairless, not shaved-looking. No beard, no moustache, no stubble, no shadow. Eyebrows thin, high and sparse.
Every one a distinct individual — different face shape, nose width, jaw, build, age from eighteen to sixty, depth of brown skin tone within the Indigenous range. No two share a face. But every one of them, without exception, is Indigenous Nahua.

THE NAHUA — CLOTHING, A STRATIFIED CITY CROWD
This is an entire city, not one class of people. The clothing must show real social range and genuine Mesoamerican textile craft.
COMMONERS, roughly half the crowd — plain undyed maguey fiber, coarse-woven, in the natural range of the plant: oatmeal, pale straw, greyish flax, warm tan, soft ochre-brown. Men in a tilmatli knotted at one shoulder hanging to the knee over a wrapped hip cloth. Women in a plain fiber huipil over a wrapped skirt. Work-worn, softened, some patched. The natural fiber tones vary noticeably person to person and the weaves differ in coarseness.
WORKING PEOPLE WITH MEANS, roughly a third — the same garments in better cloth, with woven decorative borders at the hem and neckline in simple geometric bands: stepped frets, zigzags, diamonds, chevrons, in muted natural dyes. Dull madder red, soft indigo blue, ochre yellow, black. Narrow bands, and no two patterns the same.
MERCHANTS, ARTISANS AND MINOR NOBILITY, the remainder scattered through the crowd — fine woven cotton in strong true colours. Deep cochineal crimson and rose. Rich indigo and turquoise-blue. Ochre and gold-yellow. Deep green. Warm brown-purple. Their capes and huipils carry broad elaborate woven and embroidered designs — stepped-fret bands, interlocking geometric repeats, diamond lattices, stylised flowers, butterflies, birds, serpent motifs, sun and star forms — worked in contrasting colour across the hem, the shoulders and the neckline. Some capes patterned overall rather than bordered.
ACROSS THE WHOLE CROWD: shell, bone, jade and obsidian ear ornaments and necklaces on many. Woven cord bracelets. A few with lip ornaments. Some women with coloured cloth wound into their braids.
NOBODY wears feathered headdresses, war regalia, body paint or warrior costume. These are civilians.
NOBODY is in a loincloth alone, bare-chested or bare-torsoed. Everyone is fully clothed.
The palette reads earthy and muted with genuine colour running through it — never a uniform brown mass, never a costume parade.

THE NAHUA — WHAT THEY CARRY
These people are a bereaved city, not a mob. Five weeks ago the men in that column killed their sons, husbands, brothers and daughters at the festival. The anger is grief with nowhere to go. It shows differently person to person — hard set jaws and fixed stares, some shouting themselves hoarse, some rigid and silent with fists closed, several with wet faces, men and women both, crying while they shout. Older women holding onto younger ones.

Indigenous Nahua of the Valley of Anahuac in 1520 — rich brown skin, copper to deep earth-brown, never pale and never light-skinned. THE NAHUA — CLOTHING, A STRATIFIED CITY CROWD
This is an entire city on these roofs, not one class of people. The clothing must show real social range and genuine Mesoamerican textile craft.
COMMONERS, roughly half the crowd — plain undyed maguey fiber, coarse-woven, in the natural range of the plant: oatmeal, pale straw, greyish flax, warm tan, soft ochre-brown. Men in a tilmatli knotted at one shoulder hanging to the knee over a wrapped hip cloth. Women in a plain fiber huipil over a wrapped skirt. Work-worn, softened, some patched. The natural fiber tones vary noticeably person to person and the weaves differ in coarseness.
WORKING PEOPLE WITH MEANS, roughly a third — the same garments in better cloth, with woven decorative borders at the hem and neckline in simple geometric bands: stepped frets, zigzags, diamonds, chevrons, in muted natural dyes. Dull madder red, soft indigo blue, ochre yellow, black. Narrow bands, and no two patterns the same.
MERCHANTS, ARTISANS AND MINOR NOBILITY, the remainder scattered through the crowd — fine woven cotton in strong true colours. Deep cochineal crimson and rose. Rich indigo and turquoise-blue. Ochre and gold-yellow. Deep green. Warm brown-purple. Their capes and huipils carry broad elaborate woven and embroidered designs — stepped-fret bands, interlocking geometric repeats, diamond lattices, stylised flowers, butterflies, birds, serpent motifs, sun and star forms — worked in contrasting colour across the hem, the shoulders and the neckline. Some capes patterned overall rather than bordered.
ACROSS THE WHOLE CROWD: shell, bone, jade and obsidian ear ornaments and necklaces on many. Woven cord bracelets. A few with lip ornaments. Some women with coloured cloth wound into their braids.
NOBODY wears feathered headdresses, war regalia, body paint or warrior costume. These are civilians.
NOBODY is in a loincloth alone, bare-chested or bare-torsoed. Everyone is fully clothed.
The palette reads earthy and muted with genuine colour running through it — never a uniform brown mass, never a costume parade.

THE NAHUA — WHAT THEY CARRY
These people are a bereaved city, not a mob. Five weeks ago the men in that column killed their sons, husbands, brothers and daughters at the festival. The anger is grief with nowhere to go. It shows differently person to person — hard set jaws and fixed stares, some shouting themselves hoarse, some rigid and silent with fists closed, several with wet faces, men and women both, crying while they shout. Older women holding onto younger ones.

SCENE CONTEXT
Midday under heavy overcast. Tenochtitlan, June 1520. A Spanish column comes in off the causeway and moves fast through the streets of the city toward the great pyramid. The whole city has turned out — thousands of Nahua people on the rooftops, lining the street on both sides, and packing the walkway across the canal, shouting at them from the first frame. Five weeks ago these same Spaniards butchered their families at the Toxcatl festival. Everyone here lost someone. A rock is thrown. Then dozens.

THE NAHUA — PHYSICAL APPEARANCE, CRITICAL
Every person in this crowd is a full-blooded Indigenous Nahua of central Mexico in 1520, before any European contact. Their faces are the faces of living Indigenous Nahua people from the highland communities of Puebla, Hidalgo, Tlaxcala and Guerrero — unmixed Indigenous Mexican ancestry.
SKIN: warm brown throughout, every single person — copper, russet, bronze, deep earth-brown. Nobody in this crowd is white, pale, fair-skinned, olive, Mediterranean, European, African, Black, Middle Eastern or Asian. Nobody is light-skinned. Nobody is mixed-race or mestizo. Every face is Indigenous American brown.
FACIAL HAIR: NONE WHATSOEVER ON ANY MAN. Completely smooth bare skin at the upper lip, cheeks, jaw, chin and throat — genuinely hairless, not shaved-looking. No beard, no moustache, no stubble, no goatee, no sideburns, no five o'clock shadow, no dark shading anywhere on the face. Not one man in this crowd has any facial hair at any point.
FACIAL STRUCTURE: broad face with wide prominent cheekbones set high and far apart. Broad flat forehead. Strong high-bridged nose with a wide base and full nostrils, some straight and some gently convex. Wide-set dark almond eyes with a pronounced epicanthic fold at the inner corner, irises dark brown to near-black. Full wide mouth. Heavy square jaw and a broad chin. Eyebrows thin, high and sparse.
HAIR: jet-black with a blue-black sheen, dead straight, thick and coarse, never wavy and never curled. Men wear a blunt fringe cut straight across the forehead with the rest long past the shoulders or gathered and tied at the nape. Women wear it long down the back, some braided and wound about the head with cords. Nobody has brown, blond, red or light hair. Nobody has curly, wavy or loose-textured hair.
Every one a distinct individual — different face shape, nose width, jaw, build, age from eighteen to sixty, depth of brown skin tone within the Indigenous range. No two share a face. But every one of them, without exception, is Indigenous Nahua.

THE NAHUA — CLOTHING, A STRATIFIED CITY CROWD
COMMONERS, roughly half the crowd — plain undyed maguey fiber, coarse-woven, in the natural range of the plant: oatmeal, pale straw, greyish flax, warm tan, soft ochre-brown. Men in a tilmatli knotted at one shoulder hanging to the knee over a wrapped hip cloth. Women in a plain fiber huipil over a wrapped skirt. Work-worn, softened, some patched. Fiber tones vary noticeably person to person.
WORKING PEOPLE WITH MEANS, roughly a third — the same garments in better cloth, with woven decorative borders at hem and neckline in simple geometric bands: stepped frets, zigzags, diamonds, chevrons, in muted natural dyes. Dull madder red, soft indigo blue, ochre yellow, black. No two patterns the same.
MERCHANTS, ARTISANS AND MINOR NOBILITY, the remainder scattered through — fine woven cotton in strong true colours. Deep cochineal crimson and rose. Rich indigo and turquoise-blue. Ochre and gold-yellow. Deep green. Warm brown-purple. Capes and huipils carrying broad elaborate woven and embroidered designs — stepped-fret bands, interlocking geometric repeats, diamond lattices, stylised flowers, butterflies, birds, serpent motifs, sun and star forms — worked in contrasting colour across hem, shoulders and neckline.
ACROSS THE CROWD: shell, bone, jade and obsidian ear ornaments and necklaces on many. Woven cord bracelets. A few with lip ornaments. Some women with coloured cloth wound into their braids.
NOBODY wears feathered headdresses, war regalia, body paint or warrior costume. These are civilians.
NOBODY is in a loincloth alone, bare-chested or bare-torsoed. Everyone is fully clothed.
The palette reads earthy and muted with genuine colour running through it — never a uniform brown mass, never a costume parade.

THE NAHUA — WHAT THEY CARRY
These people are a bereaved city, not a mob. Five weeks ago the men in that column killed their sons, husbands, brothers and daughters at the festival. The anger is grief with nowhere to go. Hard set jaws and fixed stares, some shouting themselves hoarse, some rigid and silent with fists closed, several with wet faces, men and women both, crying while they shout. Older women holding onto younger ones.

Midday under heavy overcast. Tenochtitlan, June 1520. A Spanish column comes in off the causeway and moves fast up a broad avenue of the city. Five weeks ago these same Spaniards butchered their families at the Toxcatl festival. Everyone here lost someone. Nothing is thrown yet. The column does not stop.

Toxcatl, the Mexica festival, in the great walled sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan,
May 1520, golden hour with the sun low and hazy behind Templo Mayor. Thousands of

raised slightly above the crowd on the steps of a small temple, two Spanish soldiers
stand watching. One of them has decided that everyone here is about to kill him. The
other is trying to talk him down without appearing to.

THE CITY — LOCATION
A broad stone-paved avenue in Tenochtitlan, wide enough for six horsemen abreast, running dead straight into the distance. Fitted stone paving, worn and dusty, no cobbles and no ruts.
Both sides of the avenue lined with tall dense buildings — two and three storeys, six to eight meters high, flat-roofed, lime-plastered white and pale cream, some with broad painted bands of red ochre and blue at the cornices, low parapet walls around every rooftop, doorways hung with plain cloth. They stand shoulder to shoulder in a continuous wall of building along both sides, tall enough that the street feels like a canyon. Between and beyond them, smaller stepped stone platforms and one or two lesser temple pyramids rising above the roofline — broad stepped platforms with a single staircase and a small square shrine on top, painted stucco. Entirely Mesoamerican and historically accurate.
THE CANAL: running parallel to the avenue on one side, separated from the roadway by a low stone kerb, a canal — a single straight channel of open water about four meters wide, cut clean through the city, faced on both sides with fitted stone banks flush with street level. Dark green-brown water, flat and still, holding a dull reflection of the overcast sky. The stonework of the banks is worn, mossy at the waterline, with a visible tide mark. One narrow dugout canoe lies moored and empty against the near bank, tied off at a stone post. No other boats anywhere. A single low stone footbridge crosses the canal far up the street. The canal runs straight and unbroken with the buildings coming right down to its far edge.
The street itself is unnaturally empty of ordinary life — no market, no traders, no children, no dogs. A few abandoned bundles and an overturned basket on the stone. The city has cleared out of the way.
In the far distance beyond the rooftops, two or three thin columns of black smoke rise straight up into the overcast from somewhere deep in the city, never from <<<image_1>>> itself.

THE NAHUA PEOPLE ON THE ROOFTOPS
Hundreds of Nahua men and women stand on the flat rooftops along both sides of the avenue, up at the low parapets, looking down at the column as it passes. They fill every roof in frame and continue up the street into the distance.
CRITICAL — HOW THEY STAND: they are standing on flat level rooftops. The roofs are flat. The people stand at the same level as one another, packed close on a flat surface, some at the parapet edge and some further back, a few crouched or seated on the parapet itself. They are NOT tiered, NOT stacked in rows rising behind one another, NOT arranged on steps or benches or bleachers. There are no seats, no stands, no stadium arrangement, no ascending rows. Just people standing on flat roofs.
They are Indigenous Nahua people of the Valley of Anahuac in 1520, pre-contact Mesoamerican, and read unmistakably as Native American of the pre-Columbian era. They are not modern, not mestizo, not Hispanic, not Latino, not Spanish, not European.
SKIN: rich brown throughout — copper, bronze, russet, deep earth-brown. Never pale, never light-skinned, never European.
FACE — every man is entirely hairless in the face. Completely smooth bare skin — bare upper lip, bare cheeks, bare jaw, bare chin, bare throat. Not clean-shaven-looking with shadow, but genuinely hairless, with no growth at all. No beard, no moustache, no stubble, no goatee, no sideburns, no five o'clock shadow, no dark shading on the jaw or upper lip. Mexica men plucked what little facial hair they had and considered it repellent; not one man in this crowd has any. Eyebrows are thin, high and sparse, plucked fine.
Broad high cheekbones set wide, wide-set almond eyes with a pronounced epicanthic fold at the inner corner, dark brown to black irises, strong high-bridged noses with broad bases, some straight and some aquiline, full mouths, square heavy jaws, broad flat foreheads, shovel-shaped front teeth when the mouth opens.
HAIR: straight, thick, coarse and jet-black with a blue-black sheen, never curled and never wavy. Men with a blunt straight fringe cut across the forehead and the rest worn long past the shoulders or gathered and tied at the nape. Women with long black hair worn loose down the back, some braided and wound about the head.
WARDROBE: fully and decently clothed. Men in a plain undyed maguey-fiber tilmatli, coarse-woven and oatmeal-grey, knotted over one shoulder and hanging to the knee, covering chest, torso and hips, over a wrapped hip cloth to mid-thigh; some in a sleeveless fiber tunic to the knee. Women in a plain fiber huipil to the knee over a wrapped skirt. Cloth undyed and work-worn, oatmeal-grey and pale brown, a few in faded dyed cloth. Simple shell or bone ear ornaments on a few. Nothing gold, nothing feathered, no headdresses, no war regalia. No loincloths, no bare chests, no bare torsos on anyone.
EXPRESSION: they are furious. Faces set hard, jaws clenched, eyes fixed and tracking the column as it passes beneath them. Many shouting, mouths wide, cords standing in the neck, leaning out over the parapets. Some silent and completely still, which is worse. Arms folded, fists at their sides, a few pointing down at the riders, one woman with her hand over her mouth.
Every one of them is a distinct individual — different face shape, nose, jaw, age from eighteen to sixty, build, hair length, depth of brown skin tone. No two of them share a face.

The causeway deck is about 20 feet across, flat worn fitted paving stone, sitting roughly
one man's height above the water, faced with cut stone capped by a flush edge course, with
a wide apron of heaped boulder riprap sloping into the water along both flanks. No parapet,
no railing, no handrail anywhere.
The road is cut clean through by a break about 25 feet across — square-cut stone end walls
dropping straight into black water on both sides of the gap, bare wet stone above them. The
drop from the water surface to the top of the lip is roughly a man's height, so a man in the
water has to reach up over his own head to get a hand on the edge course. There is no
bridge, no timber, no rope and no ladder anywhere.
The lake lies black on both flanks. No shoreline, no far bank, no city, no distant lights,
no horizon line, no land anywhere in frame.

Build it in depth layers exactly as a crowd is built: a near layer sharp on the focal band, a

Some are swimming badly. Some are treading and going under and coming up. Some have hold of

On the far side of the gap, men are hauling themselves out of the water onto the stone —

Others already out are reaching back down for the men below, hauling them up by the wrist,

A crowd is building on the far stone — soaked, on hands and knees, staggering upright,

WHAT THEY ARE: long, narrow, shallow DUGOUT CANOES — each one a single hollowed tree trunk,

What they are doing reads as movement only: standing figures driving spear shafts down into

CONDITION
The tags carry all appearance. Do not restyle, redress, re-equip or reinterpret any tagged
element. The only permitted deviation is CONDITION: every figure is soaking wet, hair
plastered flat, clothing black with water and hanging heavy, mail and quilted cotton
streaming. Men in the water are waterlogged and dragged down by mail, helmets and loads.

FORMAT MODE
Four separate static shots cut back to back. Total 16 seconds. Each cut is exactly 4 seconds.
Hard cuts, no dissolves, no fades, no transitions. Cuts only at the specified points; the
camera does not cut on its own. The camera does not move in any of the four cuts — no pan, no
tilt, no push, no drift, no handheld float. Locked off on sticks throughout.

OPTICS — HEAVY SHALLOW DEPTH OF FIELD, ALL FOUR CUTS
Long lens shot wide open in every cut. Cut 1 at 29° FOV, Cuts 2 and 3 at 18° FOV, Cut 4 at
29° FOV, set per segment with no drift mid-segment.
The focal plane is a NARROW BAND only a few feet deep, sitting six to ten feet from the lens.
One band is sharp and everything nearer and further is soft. In front of the band the falloff
is FAST. Behind it the falloff is GRADUAL — faces gone within two ranks, then rim-lit heads,
shoulders, lifted arms and hull shapes holding form deep into the frame before the mist takes
them.
Because men are moving vertically in and out of the water, figures pass IN AND OUT of focus as
they rise and sink. A man surfaces soft, sharpens as he crosses the band, and blurs as he goes
under again. Let that happen.

FOREGROUND OCCLUSION — STRICT RULES
Each cut is shot past a near-black defocused foreground element:
IT IS ALWAYS CROPPED BY THE FRAME EDGE and enters from the side or a bottom corner. It lives in
the OUTER THIRD of the frame only.
THE CENTER OF THE FRAME IS ALWAYS CLEAR. Nothing sits in the middle of the shot blocking the
subject.
IT IS NEVER A HEAD. No bare head, no skull, no scalp, no helmet crown, no face, no back of a
head anywhere in the defocused foreground layer in any cut. Only: a wet forearm or hand, a
spear shaft crossing a corner, the sloped line of a shoulder cropped at the edge, the corner of
the stone lip, or a floating pack frame entering low from the side.
It covers roughly a quarter of the frame, no more, with no face detail and no readable edge.
Rain reads at two scales: large soft blooming droplets in the defocused foreground, fine sharp
cold streaks on the focal plane.

Real-time speed. No slow motion anywhere. NOTHING IN FRAME IS STATIC AT ANY POINT.

CUT 1: the water churns for the full four seconds — men going under and surfacing, arms thrashing,

PERFORMANCE
In the water: pure animal panic. Faces tipped back to keep mouths clear, mouths wide open, gasping
and swallowing water, eyes rolling to the stone and to the men beside them. Hands grabbing anything
— cloth, mail, hair, shoulders, another man's face. No coordination, no swimming technique, no
calm. Men who go under go under fighting.
On the stone: total physical exhaustion. Chests heaving, ribs working under soaked mail,
open-mouthed retching breaths, arms shaking under their own weight, legs not holding. Wet skin at
pore level, water streaming off hair, jaws and morion brims, eyes wide and unfocused and then
snapping back to the road ahead. The men reaching down have their teeth bared with the strain of
the pull.
Running: bad running — heavy, uneven, stumbling, on legs that have nothing left.
Nobody looks at camera or reacts to camera.

PHYSICS
Heavy continuous downpour, falling dead vertical. NO WIND. Rain does not blow sideways and nothing
lifts or streams in air. Mist hangs dead still.
Water behaves with real mass — it resists, it drags, it slops heavily rather than splashing lightly.
Men in it move slowly and badly, their strength going nowhere. Mail, helmets, waterlogged quilted
cotton and pack frames pull men down; a man who stops fighting sinks. Wet mail hangs like a second
body on the men who make it out and slows every movement they make.
The surface is broken everywhere at once by rain and by bodies — chop, slop, and heavy irregular
displacement, water sheeting off heads, mail and arms as they come up.
On the stone: wet paving and a wet vertical face give almost no grip. Boots skid on the sheer stone.
Hands slip off the rounded edge course. A man being hauled up is dead weight and the man pulling him
strains visibly and slides forward on his knees.
Bodies hitting the paving land heavily and stay down. Water pours off men who come out and runs back
over the lip into the gap.
The dugouts sit low and ride heavily, pitching as men shift their weight in them and as paddles bite.

On the water it throws a broken cold glint off the disturbed surface — that glint is what makes the

The defocused foreground shapes are lit by nothing and stay near-black, broken only where the same

The stone stays dark except where the light grazes the raised edges of wet paving and the top of the

Color: the whole frame is cold blue and near-black — blue-grey wet stone, blue-white rain, blue rim

This is NOT daytime. NOT overcast daylight. NOT dusk. NOT dawn. NOT a bright storm. It is the middle

DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. Out on a great
stone causeway crossing a lake, in heavy rain and heavy mist. The road ends at a
square-cut lip with a 25-foot break of open black water in front of it. A column of a

PERFORMANCE
In the water: pure animal panic. Faces tipped back to keep mouths clear, mouths wide open,
gasping and swallowing water, eyes rolling to the stone and to the men beside them. Hands
grabbing anything — cloth, hair, shoulders, another man's face. No coordination, no swimming
technique, no calm. Men who go under go under fighting.
On the stone: total physical exhaustion. Chests heaving, ribs working, open-mouthed retching
breaths, arms shaking under their own weight, legs not holding. Wet skin at pore level, water
streaming off hair and jaws, eyes wide and unfocused and then snapping back to the road ahead.
The men reaching down have their teeth bared with the strain of the pull.
Running: bad running — heavy, uneven, stumbling, on legs that have nothing left, arms not
swinging properly.
Nobody looks at camera or reacts to camera.

The men are packed body to body with no space between them. Nobody can turn, nobody can raise an

Arrows come in relentlessly from ONE side only, flat and level, roughly TWELVE ARROWS EVERY SECOND

One second of rain and pressure and arrows. An arrow takes the soldier immediately beside them in

him. We catch one glimpse of the top of his helmet moving low between legs and hips, going the

forward, head down. Another man near them is hit and drops. López finally turns his head to check

him, and shouts his name twice. Nothing. Nobody answers. The crush keeps pushing him forward. The

lake on every side. On the near stone a mob is killing the last wounded Spaniards while fifteen
warriors shove the bridge across the paving to the edge until it goes over into the water. Three
cuts, no dialogue.

SEVENTY SPANISH DEAD lie on the causeway, on BOTH sides of the gap, and they are visible in
EVERY SINGLE CUT of this piece. There is no frame anywhere in these twelve seconds that shows
clean or empty stone.

The bridge has REAL MASS and REAL RIGIDITY. It resists. It grinds rather than slides, it moves in bursts of
a foot at a time, it shudders and stops, and it loads every man visibly. Its full weight stays on the stone
throughout — no part of it is ever lifted, held or carried.

then it tips and falls under gravity alone, with no upward or outward velocity of its own, landing FLAT and
striking all along its length at once.
Water has real mass — it drags, it slops heavily, mail and helmets pull men under, a man who stops fighting
sinks. The bridge landing throws a heavy sheet up and surges out through the men in the water.
Bodies underfoot shift and give when stepped on. Wet paving gives poor grip. Rain falls dead vertical, no
wind.

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. Out on the
great stone causeway crossing the lake, in heavy rain and heavy mist. Two mounted
commanders riding at the head of a vast retreating column reach the first breach
in the causeway — a section of the road that has been completely torn out and
removed, leaving open black water where the road used to be. They stop at the
edge. Behind them the column concertinas to a halt. No one speaks in this
sequence. Four separate locked-off setups, no dialogue, no speaking, no shouting.

THE GAP — GEOMETRY IS CRITICAL:
An entire section of the causeway has been torn out and removed. The gap runs the

severed completely. It is a total break in the road — you cannot walk around it,
past it, or along either side of it, because there is nothing there. No paving

width of the deck. Beyond that edge is roughly fourteen feet of open black lake

holding water. The road resumes at an identical square-cut edge running the whole
width of the far side. Both faces are clean dressed stone. The boulder riprap runs
along the flanks up to the break and stops.
Standing at the near edge you look across open water at the severed far end of the

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. A stone
city built on a lake, in darkness, hours before dawn. A vast column of foreign
soldiers and their allies is moving in silence out of the city and onto the great
stone causeway that crosses the lake, in heavy rain. The residents of the city
are asleep in their houses and no one has woken. This is a night scene lit by one
cold source and nothing else. Four separate locked-off setups, no dialogue, no
speaking, no shouting.

SCENE CONTEXT
Midnight, 1520, in a downpour. Where a causeway meets the western shore of Lake Texcoco,
hundreds of Spanish and Tlaxcalan survivors lie broken on the mud. A captain comes in off
the causeway on foot at the head of about twenty more, most of them wounded. One of the men
on the ground gets up, goes to him, and begs him to go back.

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. Out on a great
stone causeway crossing a lake, in heavy rain and mist. What is left of a broken army is
running on foot for the mainland — a Spanish commander and about twenty soldiers and
Tlaxcalan allies strung out along the stone at a dead run. Aztec warriors come out of the
mist directly in front of them and the run turns into a fight the commander has to cut
through without ever stopping moving. Four cuts, no dialogue.

This is a man escaping who has to keep killing to do it, and he is at the end of his body.

flicking to a movement on the flank, then forward again. Jaw clenched between breaths. His

runs on. Between strikes his face is not rage — it is a man doing arithmetic at high speed
while terrified.

water, toward the mist ahead, back over shoulders. Mouths open, shouting without words. Men
grabbing each other to stay upright.

and no fear, spears already levelled before they are visible.

SCENE CONTEXT
Night on a wide stone causeway in heavy pouring rain and thick mist. A dense Spanish

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT, 1520. Heavy rain and mist on a stone causeway over a black lake. A crossing has
fallen. The timber bridge still lies across the gap, the stone on both sides is heaped with
Spanish dead, the water is full of men drowning, and hundreds of Aztecs in canoes hold the
water on every side. On the near stone a mob is killing the last wounded Spaniards, while a
gang of warriors works the bridge sideways off its bearing to shove it into the lake. Three
cuts, no dialogue.

visibly heavy — the timber barely moves and every inch costs them.

stone the mob has not stopped.

The mob on the stone: methodical and unhurried and absolutely relentless, moving from body to body.
The Spaniards still alive: barely moving, on the ground, arms up, mouths open.
The men in the water: pure animal panic, faces tipped back to keep mouths clear, hands grabbing at

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT, 1520. Heavy rain and mist on a stone causeway over a black lake. A Spanish
commander and a handful of his men are cutting their way down the road through Aztec warriors
who keep coming at them out of the mist. He kills six men in twelve seconds and never stops
moving forward. Three cuts, close, no dialogue.

FORWARD MOTION — THE RULE THAT GOVERNS EVERYTHING
He is ESCAPING. He is trying to get down this causeway and off it, and every frame of this
piece shows him moving forward.
He is moving when each cut starts and moving when it ends. The killing happens ON THE MOVE — in
stride, or in a single checked step he is already coming out of. He never plants, never sets his
feet, never stops to fight, never squares off, never holds ground, never stands still for a
single frame. He never backs up and he never turns around.
Each man who comes at him is an obstacle in the road, not an opponent. He goes through them and
keeps going. The instant a body starts to fall he is already past it.
The camera is BEHIND him in all three cuts, on the road he has already covered. He moves AWAY
FROM THE LENS the whole time. The Aztecs are the only figures moving toward the lens.
His own men move with him, forward, in the same direction — nobody in his group turns back.

his left. Morion helmet on his head, chain mail over quilted cotton, both soaked black with
water, rain streaming off the helmet brim.
<<<a673ecd4-15ed-480b-b87b-992d4efef80d>>> and <<<bf14bbcc-f47c-497d-845b-e84ddd4e68cf>>> — the conquistadors with him, six or
eight men, morions and chain mail, swords and <<<c8064629-1ca3-44f9-9d4f-82ba76e35455>>>, fighting their own way
forward alongside him.

in from both flanks, carrying <<<a014f719-4229-4e9b-a9fe-e22667fc8cc8>>>.
<<<1fa692bc-d3a2-466d-af5d-52c97a783788>>>, <<<12663227-9345-4d28-b3bd-1c8d818091d2>>> and <<<d53388f2-d2a7-4d19-b69f-b62d12cbdedb>>> — the readable warriors among them.
Every Aztec: no helmet, hair long and straight and black and soaked flat to the head, no facial
hair, quilted cotton to mid-thigh, spear in both hands.

THE WARRIORS — THERE ARE A LOT OF THEM
This is not two men on an empty road. The causeway ahead is FULL of Aztec warriors — a press of
them filling the width of the stone and stacked back into the mist with no end visible, more of
them coming forward the whole time. Bodies overlap at every depth with no bare paving showing
between them past the first rank.
They reach him in ONES AND TWOS out of that press, breaking clear and running onto him, while
the mass behind keeps pushing forward. Behind every man he kills there are two more already
coming, and behind those, shapes in the mist that never resolve.
The impression is of a man carving a hole through a crowd that immediately closes behind him.

THE FIGHTING
HE KILLS SIX MEN. He thrusts and he slashes, all of it while moving forward.
THRUSTS: the point goes into the chest or the gut, driven by his own forward momentum with his
shoulder behind it, and he pulls the blade free as he walks through.
SLASHES: one hard flat cut, edge first, across the throat or the side of the neck, thrown as he
strides past.
No blocks, no parries, no traded blows, no clash of steel, no missed strikes. Each man dies on
the first thing done to him and none of them slows him down.
His own men are fighting too, in the background and at the edges of frame — spears going in,
shields shoving warriors aside, men going down on both sides — but soft and unreadable. He is
the only one whose kills are legible.

them going down and not getting up. They move in the same direction he does.
The warriors: fast, committed, coming out of the press at full speed with no hesitation and no fear,

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT, 1520. Heavy rain and mist on a lake. A column of Spaniards and Tlaxcalans is
trapped on a stone causeway with a broken gap ahead of it. Hundreds of Aztec canoes come out
of the mist on both sides and open fire into them. The column breaks — men shot down where
they stand, men jumping into the water, and a crowd surge that drives the front rank off the
lip into the gap. Three cuts, shot entirely from the water, no dialogue.

VANTAGE — THE RULE THAT GOVERNS EVERYTHING
Every cut is shot FROM THE CANOES, low on the water, looking UP at the causeway.
The lens sits roughly two feet above the surface, at the height of a man standing in a dugout.
The stone rises out of the water in front of it — riprap, then the cut-stone face, then the edge
course, and the column on top of it against black.
We are among the attackers. The nearest hulls, gunwales, paddles, drawn bows and the shoulders of
the men shooting are in this frame, in the near ground, mostly as SILHOUETTE. The Spaniards and
Tlaxcalans are the targets, up on the stone, at a distance.
The camera never goes up onto the causeway and never leaves the water.

THE CANOES — HUNDREDS, EMERGING
Long narrow paddled dugouts, each a single hollowed log low to the water with a plain unbroken
upper edge and nothing rising above it but the men in it. No sails, no masts, no rigging, no cloth
on any boat.
They come OUT OF THE MIST — hull shapes resolving out of black at the edge of visibility and
driving in toward the stone, layer behind layer, with more still coming out of the dark behind
those. NO CLEAR WATER is visible between hulls at any depth. The impression is HUNDREDS of boats
converging on both flanks of the causeway.
ALL OF THEM ARE SILHOUETTE except the nearest one or two: dark hulls, dark standing figures, bow
shapes and paddle blades rising above them, edge-lit along one line and black everywhere else.
<<<1207b8e8-8562-4492-bca6-75e63ce981e0>>> occupies these boats. No helmet, hair long and straight and black and
soaked flat to the head, no facial hair, quilted cotton to mid-thigh.

THE ONE WE ARE WITH
<<<1fa692bc-d3a2-466d-af5d-52c97a783788>>> is the readable warrior in the nearest boat, three to five feet from
the lens — the only figure in the water rendered in detail. Wet skin, water running off his hair
and shoulders, the cords standing out in his arm as he draws. He nocks, draws to the cheek, looses,
and reaches for the next shaft, over and over, on his own timing. Everyone else in every other boat
is silhouette doing the same thing at their own rhythm, never in unison.

THE TARGETS ON THE STONE
The column is packed on the causeway above — <<<bf14bbcc-f47c-497d-845b-e84ddd4e68cf>>> and
<<<a673ecd4-15ed-480b-b87b-992d4efef80d>>> in morion helmets and chain mail, mixed with <<<f9302e06-b1d5-4ae7-8e18-9a80cd26cfc7>>>
and <<<b02ee172-d7b7-45da-b428-a2c72ab54977>>>, bare-headed with hair soaked flat to the head, in quilted cotton to
mid-thigh, some under @prop_packframes.
They fill the width of the stone wall to wall with no ground visible between bodies, stacked back
along the road until the mist takes them, with no end to them visible.
<<<a435649f-afe2-48d2-9601-dd977c232998>>> — the men who end up in the water.
THE FRONT RANK IS TLAXCALAN and it is the front rank that goes into the gap.

THE PLACE
The causeway stands about one man's height above the water, faced with cut stone capped by a flush
edge course, with heaped boulder riprap sloping into the lake. Ahead of the column the road is cut
through by a 25-foot gap of open black water with the far segment across it. No parapet, no railing —
the stone ends and the lake begins. No shoreline, no far bank, no city, no distant lights, no horizon.

ACTION
Real-time speed. No slow motion. NOTHING IN FRAME IS STATIC.

CUT 1: the boats drive in toward the stone at 6 km/h, more of them coming out of the mist behind the
whole time. <<<1fa692bc-d3a2-466d-af5d-52c97a783788>>> nocks, draws to the cheek and looses, and reaches for the
next shaft. Up on the stone the column is packed and beginning to move wrong — heads turning toward the
water on both sides, a ripple of movement running along it. The first men are already going down.

CUT 2: the fire is continuous and scattered — bowstrings releasing all along the boats, never in unison.
Up on the stone the column comes apart: a man folds forward and drops where he stands and the mass closes
over him; another is hit and goes backward into the men behind him; men crouch, throw arms over their
heads, jam shields up toward the water; heads whip left and right looking for anywhere to go and finding
none. Then they start going in — one man throws himself off the flank into the water, then two more, then
a scattered stream of them jumping and falling and being shoved off the edge, bodies hitting the water
between the boats. The whole mass begins heaving forward along the road.

CUT 3: the surge arrives at the lip. The crowd pressure drives the front rank — <<<f9302e06-b1d5-4ae7-8e18-9a80cd26cfc7>>>
under their loads — right off the stone edge into the gap. They go in one after another and then in twos
and threes, some stepping off because there is nowhere else to be, some pushed, some falling backward with
their arms up. They hit the black water in front of the lens and go under.
<<<a435649f-afe2-48d2-9601-dd977c232998>>> surfaces close to camera, head back, one arm reaching for the stone.
Men land on top of the men already in. The lip never clears — the second the water takes one man the crush
puts another in his place. Around them the boats keep closing and the shooting does not stop.

PERFORMANCE
The men in the boats: braced, methodical, unhurried, working — feet set, bow arms steady, drawing and
loosing and reaching. They are the only figures in this piece with purpose.
The column on the stone: total panic. Bodies twisting and shoving, shoulders driving into backs, hands
grabbing at pack frames and shoulders for purchase, arms up over heads, shields jammed toward the water.
Heads whipping side to side. Mouths open, hundreds shouting without words. Men hit going down hard and
being trampled. Men in the water throwing their arms out and clutching at nothing.
Nobody looks at camera.

PHYSICS
Arrows carry real speed and drop, strike hard, bury into cloth and wood, glance off steel. Bows flex and
strings snap forward. The dugouts sit low and ride heavily, pitching as men shift their weight to shoot.
Crowd pressure behaves like a fluid — the surge PRESSES rather than strikes, weight transferring through
bodies from the back of the column forward, men lifted off their feet by the men around them.
Men entering the water break the surface hard and go under from their own weight — mail, helmets and pack
frames pull them down. Falling bodies throw heavy sheets of water up and rock the nearest hulls.
Rain falls dead vertical. No wind.

Deep moonless night. The sky is BLACK. One source only: 12000K deep blue-white, dim, low and raking across
the water, same position in all three cuts. It edges every figure and every hull down one flank and lights

NOT daytime, NOT dusk, NOT dawn, NOT a bright storm. It is the middle of a black night.

Mist density 45%, unlit. It swallows depth and turns distance to BLACK, not grey — the boats come out of
black, not out of a bright wall. It hangs dead still.

TEMPERATURE
Warm humid night, warm rain, warm water. NO VISIBLE BREATH from anyone, no vapour, no steam off wet cloth,

Fully diegetic, no music. Heavy rain on lake water, on stone, on helmet steel, on mail, on hull timber —

SCENE CONTEXT
Toxcatl, the Mexica festival, in the great walled sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan,
May 1520, golden hour with the sun low and hazy behind Templo Mayor. Thousands of
Nahuatl celebrants pack the plaza, dancing in linked rings. At the edge of the plaza,
raised slightly above the crowd on the steps of a small temple, two Spanish soldiers
stand watching. One of them has decided that everyone here is about to kill him. The
other is trying to talk him down without appearing to.

low sun, visible breath movement in the chest.

gasping, no gesturing. It is all in the unblinking stare, the darting eyes, the twitch

arithmetic — counting exits, counting his men, counting how fast. He is a man about to
do something terrible who has convinced himself it is defense. His anger at the end is
compressed rather than explosive.

word he says is chosen carefully. He is a subordinate trying to reach a superior

blowing sideways. It hammers the stone, the shields and the helmets, sheets off helmet brims in
continuous threads, runs down the shield faces, streams off shoulders and mail, and throws spray
where it strikes. Standing water on the causeway ripples and jumps under the impact. Rain reads as
fine cold streaks through the full depth of frame and as large soft blooming droplets close to the
lens. It never lets up, never thins, and never stops at any point.

CAMERA
One continuous move, slow and cinematic, no cuts. From its established position the camera pushes
forward down the line toward the third man in, descending as it goes to his eye level, and at the
same time arcing to the right around him — roughly twenty degrees past its starting angle — so
that by the end of the move we are on a three-quarter front of his face rather than his profile.
The move is smooth and unhurried, fluid head, locked horizon, no shake, no whip, no stopping. It
settles into a tight close-up: his helmet, his eyes above the shield rim, his shield filling the
lower part of frame. Once it settles, the camera comes to a complete stop and holds there,
locked and static, for the final three seconds of the shot.

ACTION
The move begins immediately. Throughout it, the shield line holds position and the men behind keep
walking down the causeway, continuous, never stopping. The mounted officer behind the line moves
his horse forward and out of frame as the camera passes. Rain keeps hammering. As the camera
settles on the third man, he is scanning out across the water, eyes moving in short hard flicks
rather than a slow sweep. The camera then holds on him, locked, for three seconds: he keeps
scanning, blinks rain out of his eyes, breathes, and keeps watching. He does not turn to camera,
does not look at it, and does not speak. The shot ends on him.

PERFORMANCE
He is not frightened. He is a soldier who has done this before — alert, wide-eyed with adrenaline
rather than fear, jaw set, breathing fast and shallow, eyes hard and tracking. Everything in him is
pointed outward at the water. Rain running off his helmet brim into his eyes; he blinks it away and
keeps watching. Small involuntary movements only, nothing performed.

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. Out on a great
stone causeway crossing a lake, in heavy rain and mist. What is left of a broken army is
running on foot for the mainland. A Spanish commander is at the front of about twenty
soldiers and Tlaxcalan allies, and Aztec warriors keep coming out of the mist in front of
him. He cuts them down as he goes and never stops running. Four cuts, close, no dialogue.

SCREEN DIRECTION — THE FIRST RULE
The entire piece is shot FROM BEHIND HIM. The camera is always on the road he has already
covered, looking down the road he is heading into. He moves AWAY FROM THE LENS in every
cut, and every man with him moves away from the lens too. The mist he is fighting into is
always at the FAR END of the frame, never behind the camera.
The warriors come out of that far mist toward him — they are the only figures in the piece
moving toward the lens.
He never turns around. He never doubles back. He never runs at the camera. Nobody in his
group runs at the camera. The direction of travel is identical in all four cuts.

THE FIGHTING — HOW IT WORKS, THE SECOND RULE
This is BUTCHERY IN MOTION, not combat between two sides.
He SWINGS AND THE MEN GO DOWN. That is the whole vocabulary. Each warrior comes out of the
mist at him, he cuts him down in one heavy stroke without breaking stride, and he keeps
going. The next one comes. He cuts that one down too.
He does not block. He does not parry. He does not catch anything on his blade. He does not
raise a shield — he is not carrying one. He does not back up, circle, sidestep, or square
off. There is never a second stroke traded between him and any man. Nobody survives his
swing long enough to answer it.
Each warrior gets ONE ARC and it is his last: the blade comes down and across, and the man
folds, drops or is driven off his feet on that single stroke and is gone from frame.
Every strike is a KILLING stroke in a straight line — down and through the neck, the
shoulder, the collarbone, the side of the head. Heavy, short, ugly, dropping the whole
weight of his body into it. No wrist work, no point work, no thrusts, no flourishes, no
recovery stance, no choreography, no rhythm of blow and counter-blow.
The warriors are pure aggression running onto a blade — they come straight at him with the
spear out in front and never bring it to bear before he cuts them down.

great stone causeway crossing the lake, in heavy rain and heavy mist. Two mounted
commanders riding at the head of a vast retreating column reach the first breach

PERFORMANCE
Nobody here is composed. These are men an hour out of something that killed most of their friends.
The men on the ground are wrung out past caring — heads down, chests heaving, some shaking
uncontrollably, one being sick into the mud, one with his hands over his face, one holding a wound
closed. They react to the arrival slowly, like men surfacing.
The arriving men are worse: limping, faltering, leaning on each other, and the moment they stop
walking they go down and stay down. Faces blank. Nobody speaks among them.
<<<ce1b4b01-1de3-460a-88b0-2c6c10b7acb0>>> says nothing at any point. He sits with his forearms on his
knees, staring at the ground, breathing hard, occasionally shivering. He lifts his head when
Guerrero arrives and watches the whole exchange without moving, without expression, too spent to
react. He never stands, never speaks, never intervenes, and he is still sitting there when the two
men walk out.
<<<ae14e9d2-59c4-4372-8c89-38c961c81add>>> is barely holding together: his face breaking open when he
recognizes him, the embrace desperate and too tight, grabbing fistfuls of his mail. Then it turns —
the grief becoming pleading, his voice climbing and cracking, hands shoving at Guerrero's shoulders,
eyes streaming with rain and not only rain. He is begging, not arguing. When Guerrero finally moves
past him, Gallego does not celebrate or react with relief — he is a beat behind, still wrecked, and
then he simply goes.
<<<952bb939-e776-4ff7-8663-34c9a2358d02>>> is emptied out. Grey, slack, unsteady on his feet, breath still
ragged. His answer is spoken to the ground. When Gallego shouts at him, nothing on his face moves
except his eyes, which stay on Gallego and do not blink. Then the eyes go to the causeway and
everything changes behind them without a word — the jaw setting, the shoulders coming up, the
breath going in. He does not announce it, does not nod, does not answer Gallego. He just turns and
walks.
Emotion reads as muscle throughout: jaws working, throats swallowing, shoulders shaking, hands
gripping and re-gripping. Pore-level skin realism and capillary flush where the skylight touches.
All figures are adults.

PHYSICS
Boots break the surface of wet mud and come out with weight. Men slip getting up. Soaked mail and
cotton hang heavy and drag on every movement. Wounded men carry their weight wrong and it shows in
the gait. Rain strikes the mud into puddles and the lake into continuous overlapping impact rings.
Haze drifts at 4 km/h.

LIGHTING
The middle of a moonless night, four hours after sunset, no fire lit anywhere. One source: a trace
of cold skylight through the cloud ceiling at 8500K, weak enough that it lands on the falling rain,
the sheen on wet mud and puddles, and a thin wet line along the tops of shoulders, morion crowns,
mail rings and cheekbones. It reaches nothing else. That thin wet line along hundreds of shoulders
and helmet crowns lying on the ground is what carries the numbers into the dark — the bodies stay
faintly readable deep into the frame long after any detail is gone. In the final cut the same thin
line along two sets of shoulders is all that holds the two walking men together as they recede.
Faces sit mostly below that line and are barely separable from the dark, readable in the close-ups
only in the fraction the light catches. Eighty-five percent of the frame carries no information.
Heavily underexposed, murky, unresolved, and the exposure never lifts.

COLOR GRADE
Near-monochrome, crushed hard toward black with a faint cold cast. Nothing in frame reads as a

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. A stone
city built on a lake, in darkness, hours before dawn. A vast column of foreign
soldiers and their allies is moving in silence out of the city and onto the great
stone causeway that crosses the lake, in heavy rain. The residents of the city
are asleep in their houses and no one has woken. This is a night scene lit by one
cold source and nothing else. Four separate locked-off setups, no dialogue, no
speaking, no shouting.

LOCATION MAP
The waterfront edge of the city where the great causeway leaves it. Three zones:
a broad open paved QUAY running perpendicular across the water's edge; the CITY
STREETS feeding into that quay from behind; and the CAUSEWAY itself, launching
from the quay at a T-junction and running out straight across black open water.
No building stands at the mouth of the causeway and nothing flanks it — the
causeway begins in open ground at a plain stone threshold with no gate and no
arch.
The causeway deck is about 12 meters across and sits roughly one man's height

apron of heaped boulder riprap sloping into the water on both sides. No parapet,

plain rectangular doorways with square lintels, painted horizontal bands of dark

FORMAT MODE
Four separate static shots cut back to back. Total 12 seconds. Each cut is
exactly 3 seconds. Hard cuts, no dissolves, no fades, no transitions. The camera
does not move in any of the four cuts — no pan, no tilt, no push, no drift, no

OPTICS
Cuts 1, 2 and 3 are long lens — 75mm equivalent, shot wide open, compressed
perspective. The telephoto flattens depth and stacks heads vertically on top of
one another so the crowd reads as a solid wall of bodies rising up the frame
rather than a line of people spaced out along a road. Shallow depth of field, the
focal plane on one narrow band of figures roughly ten to fifteen feet from
camera. Everything behind it goes progressively soft, loses face detail, becomes
only rim-lit shapes and rising spear shafts, and finally dissolves into rain and
blackness. The dissolve is GRADUAL — never a hard cutoff. The receding mass must
stay faintly readable deep into the frame because that depth is what sells the
numbers.
Cut 4 is the exception: a wide elevated view where scale, not lens compression,
carries the mass. Deep focus, everything sharp to the mid-distance, the far
causeway softening into rain.

SCENE CONTEXT
DEEP NIGHT. Moonless, black sky, no daylight of any kind. Night, 1520. Out on a great
stone causeway crossing a lake, in heavy rain and mist. A wide break in the road has
become a drowning pit — the black water in the gap is packed with hundreds of Spaniards
and Tlaxcalans struggling, going under and clawing at each other, while the far stone lip
is crowded with men dragging themselves out. Across the gap, the side they came from is
covered in dead and men still fighting. All around, hundreds of war canoes work the water.
Four cuts, no dialogue. Close coverage throughout.

SPANISH WARDROBE — STRICT
Every Spaniard in this piece wears a MORION HELMET on his head and CHAIN MAIL on his body.
The morion is steel, one piece, with a fore-and-aft comb along the crown and a curved brim
front and back, streaming rainwater off both points. The mail is a shirt of fine riveted
iron rings covering torso and upper arms, worn over a quilted garment, hanging heavy and
soaking wet, the individual rings catching the cold light in a fine broken texture along
one flank.
This is true of <<<bf14bbcc-f47c-497d-845b-e84ddd4e68cf>>>, <<<a673ecd4-15ed-480b-b87b-992d4efef80d>>> and
<<<a435649f-afe2-48d2-9601-dd977c232998>>> alike, in the water and on the stone — the men climbing out are
climbing in mail, and that is exactly why it is so hard for them. Helmets stay on heads.
Mail stays on bodies. No bare heads among the Spanish, no cloth-only torsos, no exposed
shirtsleeves.
The Tlaxcalans are the opposite and stay that way: BARE-HEADED, long straight black hair
soaked flat to the skull, no facial hair, quilted cotton war jackets to mid-thigh, no
helmets of any kind, no mail, no shields.

THE PLACE
The causeway deck is about 20 feet across, flat worn fitted paving stone, sitting roughly
one man's height above the water, faced with cut stone capped by a flush edge course, with
a wide apron of heaped boulder riprap sloping into the water along both flanks. No parapet,
no railing, no handrail anywhere.
The road is cut clean through by a break about 25 feet across — square-cut stone end walls
dropping straight into black water on both sides of the gap. The drop from the water surface
to the top of the lip is roughly a man's height, so a man in the water has to reach up over
his own head to get a hand on the edge course. There is no bridge, no timber, no rope and no
ladder anywhere.
The lake lies black on both flanks. No shoreline, no far bank, no city, no distant lights,
no horizon line, no land anywhere in frame.

PERFORMANCE
In the water: pure animal panic. Faces tipped back to keep mouths clear, mouths wide open, gasping
and swallowing water, eyes rolling to the stone and to the men beside them. Hands grabbing anything —
cloth, mail, hair, shoulders, another man's face. No coordination, no swimming technique, no calm.
Men who go under go under fighting.
On the stone: total physical exhaustion. Chests heaving, ribs working under soaked mail, open-mouthed
retching breaths, arms shaking under their own weight, legs not holding. Wet skin at pore level,
water streaming off hair, jaws and morion brims, eyes wide and unfocused and then snapping back to
the road ahead. The men reaching down have their teeth bared with the strain of the pull.
Across the gap: the fighting is exhausted and desperate, not skilled — short heavy movements, men
grappling and shoving as much as striking, nobody holding a line.
Running: bad running — heavy, uneven, stumbling, on legs that have nothing left.
Nobody looks at camera or reacts to camera.

PHYSICS
Heavy continuous downpour, falling dead vertical. NO WIND. Rain does not blow sideways and nothing
lifts or streams in air. Mist hangs dead still.
Water behaves with real mass — it resists, it drags, it slops heavily rather than splashing lightly.
Men in it move slowly and badly, their strength going nowhere. Mail, helmets, waterlogged quilted
cotton and pack frames pull men down; a man who stops fighting sinks. Wet mail hangs like a second
body on the men who make it out and slows every movement they make.
The surface is broken everywhere at once by rain and by bodies — chop, slop, and heavy irregular
displacement, water sheeting off heads, mail and arms as they come up.
On the stone: wet paving and a wet vertical face give almost no grip. Boots skid on the sheer stone.
Hands slip off the rounded edge course. A man being hauled up is dead weight and the man pulling him
strains visibly and slides forward on his knees.
Bodies hitting the paving land heavily and stay down. Bodies going off the far edge fall a man's
height and break the surface hard. Water pours off men who come out and runs back over the lip into
the gap.
The dugouts sit low and ride heavily, pitching as men shift their weight in them and as paddles bite.
